transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Good morning, Mr Ashdown-Pryce. I'm Dr Nwosu from the respiratory team. And you've brought...?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: My wife, Valerie.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: Hello.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Lovely. How have things been since we last saw you?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Not great. I'm more breathless. I have to stop halfway up the hill to the shops now.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: How about on the flat?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I can walk on the flat at my own pace, but I'm slower than Valerie.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any cough or phlegm?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: A cough most mornings, with white phlegm.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: How many flare-ups have you had in the last year, where you needed steroid tablets or antibiotics?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Two. One in January, and one in the summer.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Both needed prednisolone?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yes, both times. The summer one needed antibiotics as well.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any hospital admissions?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any swelling in your ankles?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: That's me. I'm the one with the swollen ankles. His are fine.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Thanks, Valerie. Any chest pain, or coughing up blood?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any weight loss?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, I've been steady.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: And you stopped smoking, is that right?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Six months ago. I haven't had one since.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Well done, that's the single best thing you can do. How much did you smoke, and for how long?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Twenty a day for forty years. Well, I stopped for ten years in the middle, so thirty years.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Thirty, then. What inhalers are you using?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: The Anoro one, once a day. And the blue one, maybe twice a day.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Can you show me how you use the Anoro?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: (demonstrates)

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: That's good technique. Have you had your flu jab and the pneumonia jab?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Both, at the surgery.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any other medicines? Allergies?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Just the inhalers. No allergies.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Let me examine you. Your oxygen level is 93 percent on air. Your breathing rate is 20. Let me listen. There's some wheeze on both sides, and some coarse crackles at the bottom of your left lung, at the left base.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Is that new?

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: It wasn't noted last time. Your breathing test today shows an FEV1 of 52 percent of predicted, a bit lower than last year. And your blood eosinophil count last month was 0.35.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: What does that mean?

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: It means you might benefit from adding a steroid to your inhalers, because you're still having flare-ups. I'd like to switch the Anoro to Trelegy, one puff once a day. It has the same two medicines plus an inhaled steroid.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: I'd also like to refer you to pulmonary rehabilitation. It's an exercise and education programme, and it really helps with breathlessness.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I've heard of it. I'll give it a go.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Because of the crackles at the left base, I'd like a chest X-ray today, before you go.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: I'll see you back in clinic in three months.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Thank you.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: If you have a flare-up, with more breathlessness, more phlegm or a change in its colour, contact your GP the same day. If you're very breathless, call 999.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay.

reference_note.history: MRC dyspnoea grade 3. Morning cough with white sputum. Two exacerbations requiring oral steroids in the last 12 months (one also needed antibiotics); no hospital admissions. No ankle swelling. No chest pain, haemoptysis or weight loss. Ex-smoker for 6 months, approximately 30 pack-years. Good inhaler technique with Anoro. Had flu and pneumococcal vaccines.
reference_note.medications_allergies: Anoro Ellipta (umeclidinium/vilanterol) one inhalation once daily. Salbutamol as needed (about twice daily). No known drug allergies.
reference_note.examination: SpO2 93% on air, RR 20. Bilateral wheeze. Coarse crackles at the left base (new). Spirometry: FEV1 52% predicted (lower than last year). Blood eosinophils 0.35 × 10⁹/L.
reference_note.impression: COPD with frequent exacerbations despite LAMA/LABA; eosinophils ≥0.3, suitable for triple therapy. New focal crackles at the left base.
reference_note.plan: Switch Anoro to Trelegy Ellipta one inhalation once daily. Refer to pulmonary rehabilitation. Chest X-ray today. Clinic review in 3 months.
reference_note.safety_netting: Contact GP the same day if increased breathlessness, sputum volume or change in sputum colour. Call 999 if severely breathless.
